findings.title: Bottleneck is likely upstream of the array
findings.body: Front-end metrics are degraded while every back-end signal this vendor publishes is within range. That points to the network/fabric path as the likely cause rather than the array's internal components.
investigate: Check switch/fabric port counters (CRC errors, discards, link resets) on the paths between hosts and this array over the same window.
Confirm host HBA/NIC driver and firmware versions, and multipath (MPIO) failover state — a path flapping in and out looks like latency at the array.
Compare front-end latency against SAN/network device queue depth, buffer-credit exhaustion (FC), or NIC ring-buffer drops (iSCSI/NFS), if your fabric monitoring exposes them.
Correlate the timing of the front-end degradation against any recent zoning, switch firmware, or network maintenance changes.
remediate: Engage the network/SAN team first — this is very likely their path, not an array-side fix.
If a specific fabric link or interface is implicated, reseat/replace the SFP or cable and re-test.
Re-balance or fail back multipath sessions once the network layer is confirmed stable.
If no path issue is found, remember this vendor's public back-end metrics may not cover every internal component — don't rule the array out on back-end panels alone before engaging vendor support.

findings.title: Volume Latency (avg)
findings.body: Average volume latency is 17.2ms — NetApp's own guidance treats sustained latency in this range as workload-impacting for most applications.
investigate: Check the breakdown below for which specific volume(s) are driving the average.
Check whether the affected volume(s) share an aggregate with a workload showing high disk or CPU busy (see the back-end panels).
Review QoS policy groups for the affected volumes — a throughput/IOPS ceiling can present as latency.
Check the volume_avg_latency_read/volume_avg_latency_write panels below — a one-sided spike often points to a specific workload, not the cluster generally.
remediate: If a specific volume is responsible, review or adjust its QoS policy group limits.
If the underlying aggregate's disks or the node's CPU are also elevated, address that back-end resource rather than the volume in isolation.
Consider moving the volume to a less-contended aggregate or node if the imbalance persists.

findings.title: Volume Latency — Read
findings.body: Average read latency is 16.9ms — a read-isolated spike often points to cache misses or a specific workload, not the cluster broadly.
investigate: If write latency is clean but read latency isn't, check for a cold working set or a change in read pattern for the affected volume(s).
Correlate against aggr_disk_busy — a read latency spike with high disk busy points to the media/aggregate, not the network path.
remediate: If isolated to specific volumes, review their read-cache sizing and working-set fit before treating this as a cluster-wide issue.
If broad and correlated with back-end signals, treat as a general cluster issue — see the combined volume_avg_latency finding's remediation.

findings.title: Volume Latency — Write
findings.body: Average write latency is 17.2ms — a write-isolated spike often points to snapshot/dedup/replication activity competing for the write path, not the cluster broadly.
investigate: If read latency is clean but write latency isn't, check recent snapshot schedules, dedup/compression scans, or SnapMirror activity.
Correlate against node_cpu_busy and aggr_disk_busy — a write latency spike with both clean points to the network path, not the array.
remediate: If correlated with background jobs, reschedule them to a lower-impact window rather than tuning the write path directly.
If broad and correlated with back-end signals, treat as a general cluster issue — see the combined volume_avg_latency finding's remediation.

findings.title: NIC Utilization (max port)
findings.body: A network port is at 96% utilization — a failover event would likely saturate the remaining path.
investigate: Identify which physical port is at high utilization and which LIFs/workloads are bound to it.
Check whether traffic is evenly distributed across available ports (ifgrp/LACP) or concentrated on one link.
Confirm current failover capacity — what utilization would result if a partner port failed over onto this one.
remediate: Rebalance LIFs across available physical ports if traffic is unevenly distributed.
Add additional network ports/interface group members if the cluster has outgrown current bandwidth.
Schedule any planned failover testing for a low-traffic window until headroom is restored.

findings.title: NIC CRC / Receive Errors
findings.body: NIC CRC error rate is 6.5/min — an actively degrading link, not cluster load.
investigate: Identify the specific port from the array's own per-port error breakdown.
Check the physical layer: cable, SFP, and the switch port's own error counters.
Review recent cabling, SFP, or switch-side changes.
remediate: Reseat or replace the cable/SFP on the affected port.
Engage the network team if the switch-side port also reports errors.
Fail the LIF over to a healthy port while the link is repaired.

findings.title: S3 Operation Failure Rate
findings.body: S3 operations are failing at 17/min — check client error codes (4xx vs 5xx) to narrow down auth vs. server-side causes.
investigate: Break down failures by HTTP status code (4xx vs. 5xx) — 4xx points to client/auth issues, 5xx to the grid itself.
Check whether failures are concentrated on specific buckets, tenants, or client IPs.
Correlate against node CPU and metadata query latency for the same window (see back-end/front-end panels).
remediate: For 4xx-dominant failures, work with the affected client/tenant on credentials or request formatting — this isn't a grid-health issue.
For 5xx-dominant failures correlating with node load, address the underlying resource pressure on that node.
Escalate to NetApp support if 5xx errors persist with no clear resource cause.

findings.title: Network Interface Errors
findings.body: Network interface errors are occurring (2.88/min) — industry practice treats any sustained nonzero rate as a physical-layer fault, not background noise. Check cabling/NIC health on this node.
investigate: Use this panel's per-node breakdown to identify the specific node, then check its interface-level counters directly.
Check the physical layer: cable, NIC, and the switch port's own error counters.
Review recent cabling, NIC, or switch-side changes on this node.
remediate: Reseat or replace the cable/NIC on the affected interface.
Engage the network team if the switch-side port also reports errors.
Monitor client-facing error rates on this node while the link is repaired, since StorageGRID load balancing may route around it.

findings.title: ILM Evaluation Backlog
findings.body: 454,172 objects are awaiting ILM evaluation — a growing backlog here is an early signal of a node falling behind, before it shows up as client latency.
investigate: Use this panel's per-node breakdown to see whether the backlog is isolated to one node or spread grid-wide, and whether it correlates with recent ingest bursts.
Review ILM policy complexity — policies with many placement rules or evaluation criteria take longer per object.
Confirm this node's CPU and metadata latency aren't independently elevated and causing the backlog as a side effect.
remediate: If ingest-burst driven and temporary, monitor — the backlog should drain once ingest returns to normal.
If policy-driven, simplify the ILM policy's evaluation logic where possible.
If node resource-constrained, address the underlying CPU/latency issue first; the backlog is usually a symptom, not the root cause.

findings.title: Storage Capacity Used
findings.body: Storage capacity is at 86% used, above the 80% guidance.
investigate: Use this panel's per-node breakdown to see which node is closest to full, then break down its usage by tenant/bucket to identify what's driving growth.
Check ILM policy placement — verify objects are being tiered/erasure-coded as intended rather than left in a more space-intensive state.
Review ingest-rate trend over the reporting window (7D/30D) to project time-to-full.
remediate: Expand storage capacity (additional nodes/volumes) if growth is sustained and expected to continue.
Review and correct ILM policy if objects aren't reaching their intended, more space-efficient placement tier.
Engage the responsible tenant if a single tenant's growth is disproportionate.

findings.title: Metadata Query Latency — mock-sg-grid-01-dc1-s2
findings.body: The fleet-wide average for this metric reads good, but mock-sg-grid-01-dc1-s2 is masking that: Metadata query latency is averaging 101ms, above the 50ms illustrative guidance — client-facing S3/Swift requests will feel this. This platform's redundancy (replication/erasure coding, quorum reads, or load-balanced traffic, depending on the metric) typically contains the impact to whatever happens to touch this specific node — check whether other nodes show the same symptom before treating it as grid-wide.
investigate: Check this node's Cassandra/metadata service health and compaction activity — metadata latency often traces back there.
Confirm this node's CPU utilization (see the back-end panel) — a busy node commonly shows up first as metadata latency.
Use this panel's per-node breakdown to see whether the latency is isolated to one node or grid-wide.
remediate: If isolated to one node, investigate that node's local resource pressure (CPU, disk I/O) directly.
If grid-wide, review recent ingest-volume growth against the grid's provisioned metadata capacity.
Engage NetApp support with a case if metadata service errors are also present in the node's logs.

findings.title: Node CPU Utilization — mock-sg-grid-01-dc1-s1
findings.body: The fleet-wide average for this metric reads good, but mock-sg-grid-01-dc1-s1 is masking that: Node CPU utilization is averaging 76%, above the 70% sustained guidance. This platform's redundancy (replication/erasure coding, quorum reads, or load-balanced traffic, depending on the metric) typically contains the impact to whatever happens to touch this specific node — check whether other nodes show the same symptom before treating it as grid-wide.
investigate: Use this panel's per-node breakdown to find which node is hottest, then identify which service (LDR, ADC, CMN, metadata) is consuming its CPU.
Check for a recent increase in ingest rate, ILM policy complexity, or scan/verification jobs.
Compare the breakdown across nodes in the same site to see if load is unevenly distributed.
remediate: Rebalance client/load-balancer traffic away from this node if others have more headroom.
Simplify or reschedule ILM policy evaluation if it's a major CPU contributor.
If sustained grid-wide, this is a capacity signal — plan additional storage nodes.

findings.title: Node CPU Busy — mock-ontap-cluster-03-node-1
findings.body: The fleet-wide average for this metric reads good, but mock-ontap-cluster-03-node-1 is masking that: Node CPU busy is averaging 91% — the controller itself is now a contributing factor, not just the path to it. This platform has no automatic way to route around a bad node for this resource, so the impact is real and current for whatever this node is hosting right now — not just a statistic.
investigate: Check the node's own per-process CPU domain breakdown (`node run -node <node> sysstat -x` or ONTAP System Manager's Performance view) for what's actually consuming cycles.

Check whether both nodes in an HA pair are elevated, or only one (possible uneven workload distribution).
remediate: Rebalance volumes/workloads across nodes in the HA pair if one node is consistently hotter.
Reschedule CPU-intensive background jobs (dedup, compression scans) to off-peak hours.
If sustained cluster-wide, this is a capacity signal — plan a controller upgrade or additional node.

findings.title: Aggregate Disk Busy — disk-1
findings.body: The fleet-wide average for this metric reads good, but disk-1 is masking that: Aggregate disk busy is averaging 91% — the backing disks are the likely bottleneck, not the network path. This platform has no automatic way to route around a bad node for this resource, so the impact is real and current for whatever this node is hosting right now — not just a statistic.
investigate: Identify which aggregate and which volumes on it are driving disk activity.
Check the aggregate's RAID group health — a degraded/rebuilding RAID group significantly raises disk busy.
Review recent growth in random I/O workloads, which stress disk busy more than sequential ones.

findings.body: The fleet-wide average for this metric reads good, but mock-sg-grid-03-dc1-adm1 is masking that: Node CPU utilization is averaging 89% — the node itself is now a contributing factor to any client-facing slowness. investigate: Use this panel's per-node breakdown to find which node is hottest, then identify which service (LDR, ADC, CMN, metadata) is consuming its CPU.
Check for a recent increase in ingest rate, ILM policy complexity, or scan/verification jobs.
Compare the breakdown across nodes in the same site to see if load is unevenly distributed.
remediate: Rebalance client/load-balancer traffic away from this node if others have more headroom.
Simplify or reschedule ILM policy evaluation if it's a major CPU contributor.
If sustained grid-wide, this is a capacity signal — plan additional storage nodes.
